enrichment.short_title: CCRC murder reference and undisclosed witness convictions
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of murder in 1995 after Terry McPherson was killed in Teignmouth; the prosecution case was largely circumstantial.
Micky Lewis gave evidence of a post-offence confession, but his 54 previous convictions (39 for dishonesty) were not disclosed because he gave a false name and date of birth.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case; fresh pathologist and DNA evidence were also considered.
The court held Lewis's evidence went to a subsequent confession, not the central circumstantial facts, and dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission to the Court of Appeal against conviction following refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the conviction was held to be safe despite non-disclosure of the witness's previous convictions.
enrichment.ratio: Non-disclosure of a prosecution witness's previous convictions does not automatically render a conviction unsafe; the court must assess whether the undisclosed material might reasonably have affected the jury's verdict, and where other evidence is compelling the omission of a confession witness's bad character may be immaterial.
legal_issues: Effect of non-disclosure of a prosecution witness's previous convictions on the safety of a conviction
Whether Micky Lewis's evidence went to the heart of the case or only to an alleged confession
Admissibility and weight of fresh pathologist evidence on time of death
Whether fresh DNA evidence affected the safety of the conviction

confidence.notes: Long full-text judgment with detailed factual findings and clear disposal on the main CCRC ground.

enrichment.short_title: Reinsurance non-disclosure and truth of media allegations
key_facts: London reinsurers sought declarations that they had validly avoided reinsurances of Colombian insurers covering a state-owned bank.
The reinsureds had not disclosed Colombian media reports and investigations alleging corruption involving the bank's president, S. Benjamin Medina.
Moore-Bick J struck out defence paragraphs denying actual misconduct; the reinsureds appealed, arguing truth of the allegations should be tried.
The Court of Appeal held materiality is judged at placement by reference to information then known, not by later proof that allegations were false.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited appeal with permission against an order striking out parts of the defence in reinsurance avoidance proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; reinsureds debarred from adducing evidence on whether there was actual misconduct justifying the investigations.
enrichment.ratio: In insurance and reinsurance, the duty of disclosure requires disclosure of material intelligence known at the time of placement; whether undisclosed allegations or investigations were later shown to be unfounded does not determine materiality or validate avoidance, and insurers need not litigate the truth of rumours before rescinding for non-disclosure.
legal_issues: Whether materiality of non-disclosed media reports depends on whether allegations of misconduct were true
Whether reinsurers' avoidance could be defeated by proving at trial that investigations were politically motivated
Application of Pan Atlantic inducement and materiality tests to moral hazard and intelligence
Whether Colman J's reasoning in The Grecia Express should be followed

enrichment.short_title: Mandatory lifer Parole Board review interval challenge
key_facts: Mr Spence, a mandatory life prisoner recalled several times for licence breaches and alcohol-related offending, was recommended for transfer to open conditions.
The Parole Board recommended the next review begin nine months after transfer; the Secretary of State substituted eighteen months.
Judicial review was refused at first instance; the prisoner appealed on lawfulness, Article 5(4), and irrationality grounds.
By the time of the appeal the review interval had effectively been shortened administratively, but the court dismissed the appeal on the merits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision on timing of the next Parole Board review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Secretary of State lawfully fixed an eighteen-month interval before the next review.
enrichment.ratio: The Home Secretary may depart from a Parole Board recommendation on when a mandatory lifer's next review should begin if individual reasons justify a longer testing period; Article 5(4) requires reasonable review intervals assessed prospectively, not prescriptive speed, and reasonableness is for the court rather than Wednesbury review alone.
legal_issues: Whether the executive may delay the start of a post-tariff mandatory lifer's next Parole Board review
Whether an eighteen-month interval before review breached Article 5(4) ECHR
Whether the Secretary of State irrationally applied a blanket July 1998 policy
Whether the Parole Board has power to defer answering referral questions

enrichment.short_title: Roundabout design negligence and motorcycle collision
key_facts: Mr King rode his motorcycle at about 2 am into the central island of the Cobtree roundabout near Maidstone, colliding with chevron signs.
The trial judge found the highway authority negligent in designing too high an entry angle with insufficient deflection, and apportioned contributory negligence at 50%.
The authority appealed on negligence, causation, and contributory negligence.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal 2-1, holding the accident was caused by the claimant's failure to observe give-way markings and signs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a High Court judgment finding highway authority negligence and 50% contributory negligence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the claimant's claim was set aside for want of causation and negligence.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a roundabout approach may exceed recommended entry angles, a highway authority is not liable if an attentive driver had ample warning of the roundabout and the accident was caused by the claimant's failure to notice give-way lines, hazard markings, and turn-left signs rather than by the design defect.
legal_issues: Whether excessive entry angle and lack of deflection breached the highway authority's duty of care
Whether any design breach caused the accident
Proper apportionment of contributory negligence
Relevance of post-accident safety audit recommendations

enrichment.short_title: Dublin safe third country policy and daughter's asylum claim
key_facts: The claimant, a Kosovan asylum seeker, was to be returned to Italy under the Dublin Convention after his wife's asylum claim was refused.
A July 2002 policy change limited family-tie discretion to dependants still awaiting an initial asylum decision.
His daughter Elida had lodged a separate asylum application in October 2001 which had not yet received an initial decision.
The Secretary of State argued Elida was covered by her mother's refused dependant application; the court rejected that construction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second application for judicial review following permission granted on one ground relating to construction of the safe third country family-ties policy.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review succeeded; the July 2002 decision was quashed but the court declined to order substantive consideration, remitting reconsideration to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: Under the 2002 safe third country family-ties policy, an unmarried minor child included only as a dependant in a principal's refused claim is not treated as having received an initial decision on her own asylum claim; a later free-standing application by the child can engage paragraph (c) of the policy if no initial decision has yet been made.
legal_issues: True construction of the July 2002 family-ties discretion policy
Whether the Secretary of State's construction was reasonably open to him
Interaction between rule 349 dependant inclusion and separate asylum claims
Whether the court should order substantive consideration or only quash

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 immigration appeal and proportionality review
key_facts: Ms Edore, an overstayer from Nigeria, had two children in the UK fathered by a married British citizen who saw them weekly and provided support.
A special adjudicator allowed her section 65 appeal as removal would be disproportionate under Article 8.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal reversed, treating interference as flowing from the father's choice and finding removal proportionate.
The Court of Appeal restored the adjudicator, holding the Secretary of State's decision was outside the range of reasonable responses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission to consider the approach to section 65 human rights appeals and proportionality.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT decision set aside and adjudicator's decision of 20 June 2002 restored.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 65 appeal the adjudicator asks whether the Secretary of State's removal decision was within the range of reasonable responses in striking a fair Article 8 balance, not whether the adjudicator would prefer a different outcome; nevertheless removal may be quashed where, on undisputed facts, only one proportionate conclusion is reasonably open.
legal_issues: Correct approach of adjudicators and the IAT to proportionality under section 65
Whether appellate authorities may substitute their preferred Article 8 balance
Whether removal interfered with family life or only reflected the father's refusal to relocate
Whether removal of the appellant and her children was proportionate on the facts

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 and return after unlawful removal to Germany
key_facts: The claimant applied for permission to judicially review removal of his family to Germany on 25 February 2003.
Hooper J had already found the removal arguably unlawful and adjourned whether the court would order return to enable civil claims.
The claimant proposed claims including alleged assaults by immigration officers on 15 August 2002.
The Secretary of State certified that Article 6 did not arguably require the family's presence in the UK to pursue those claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review on whether failure to return the family would breach Article 6.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; the Secretary of State's Article 6 certificate was not arguably wrong.
enrichment.ratio: At an early stage of proposed civil proceedings, Article 6 does not arguably require a removed claimant to remain in the United Kingdom where witness statements, medical records, and police statements already exist and overseas lawyers or limited further instructions would suffice, especially where the main live claim concerns a brief assault incident.
legal_issues: Whether unlawful removal must be remedied by ordering return to pursue civil proceedings
Whether Article 6 requires presence in the UK to conduct proposed claims with reasonable sufficiency
Effect of the Secretary of State's section 72-style certificate on in-country appeal rights
Whether the claimant's solicitors' witness statement established need for detailed in-person instructions

confidence.notes: Transcript-style judgment continuing an earlier ruling; focused on one Article 6 issue with clear refusal of permission.

enrichment.short_title: Harry Potter leak injunction against persons unknown
key_facts: Copies of Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix were taken without authority from secure printers and offered to national newspapers.
Interim injunctions had been made against persons unknown who offered copies to the Sun, Daily Mail, and Daily Mirror.
Named defendants were arrested or submitted to orders; the issue was continuing the injunction against unidentified persons.
The Vice-Chancellor held CPR permitted defendants described with sufficient certainty and continued the order until publication.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application to continue ex parte injunctions against unnamed defendants pending publication of the fifth Harry Potter book.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction continued until 21 June 2003 against persons described as those offering or possessing copies without the claimants' consent.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Civil Procedure Rules a claimant may sue and obtain injunctions against defendants identified by a sufficiently certain description rather than by name, where the description identifies who is bound and who is not; Friern Barnet and Re Wykeham Terrace are not applicable to CPR proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether unnamed defendants may be joined under the Civil Procedure Rules
Whether the proposed description was sufficiently certain
Whether orders against persons unknown would bind anyone in contempt proceedings
Distinction from McPhail v Persons Unknown and Friern Barnet UDC v Adams

confidence.notes: Full Chancery judgment with detailed procedural analysis and clear order.

enrichment.short_title: Guilty plea set aside after undisclosed sensitive material
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty at Croydon Crown Court to being knowingly concerned in importing cocaine after swallowing 90 packages at Gatwick.
She was sentenced to three years' imprisonment and had been advised a duress defence might succeed but chose to plead guilty.
Customs later disclosed sensitive material that would have attracted public interest immunity and likely led to no prosecution or an offered no-evidence submission.
The Court of Appeal granted an extension of time, allowed the appeal, and set aside the guilty plea.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Out-of-time application for leave to appeal against conviction following late disclosure by Customs and Excise.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed and guilty plea set aside.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal against conviction may succeed despite a guilty plea where undisclosed prosecution material was so sensitive that the prosecution would not have proceeded or would have offered no evidence, and the appellant would have been strongly advised not to plead guilty had the material been available.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal will entertain an appeal after a guilty plea
Whether non-disclosure of sensitive material meant the appellant did not have a fair trial
Effect of public interest immunity on prosecution disclosure obligations
Whether pragmatic reasons for pleading guilty prevent setting aside the plea

confidence.notes: Short judgment; sensitive material deliberately not described but legal principles clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Rural housing appeal and PPG3 sustainability
key_facts: Developers appealed refusal of planning permission to demolish a garage and coach depot and build five houses at Stiperstones in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
The council refused mainly because the village was not a sustainable settlement under PPG3 and its Interim Housing Policy.
A planning inspector allowed the appeal, treating the scheme as modest infill meeting paragraphs 69 and 71 of PPG3.
The council challenged the decision on five grounds including development plan compliance, bus service evidence, and interim policy weight.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to a planning inspector's appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the inspector's grant of permission was upheld on all five grounds.
enrichment.ratio: An inspector lawfully may find a five-house infill scheme in a small village consistent with PPG3 rural housing policy despite conflict with local plan policies limiting infill to one or two dwellings, and may give limited weight to an interim housing policy that exceeds national guidance where it has not been publicly consulted upon.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to address development plan conflict with Policies HG4 and STI1
Whether relocation of a bus depot would terminate the village bus service
Whether the Interim Housing Policy was incompatible with PPG3
Whether the inspector adequately reasoned that the scheme satisfied a local housing requirement
Whether finding the site sustainable was perverse

confidence.notes: Detailed planning judgment addressing five grounds systematically; transcript includes costs argument.
